Cursor: request flow and controls

The step-by-step guide explains each step in general; how to read these trees.

What happens to a request

The steps run in the typical order. A documented order, where the vendor states one, is shown on its step. A decision point appears where the documentation describes a real branch; an agent with none has none documented.

A. Setup, before the first model call

The harness gets ready: it finds your rules, your tools and your permissions. No model is involved yet.

  1. Choose the front door ● documented !

    You can reach Cursor from a terminal, from JetBrains editors, from its own editor and agents window, from a browser, from a script or code library, and from chat and code-hosting tools such as Slack, Teams and GitHub comments.

  2. Apply organization rules ◐ documented, with limits !

    Companies can deploy Cursor with enforced policies through device management, and team hooks sync from a dashboard, though managed hooks need Enterprise. Locking network access and limiting models or MCP servers are Enterprise features; a team review setting takes priority.

    Documented order: A team-defined global automatic-review setting takes priority, and Cursor ignores user-level and project-level files.

    Decision point: What happens when an admin blocks a model for the team?

    • A model is blocked for the team: On Enterprise, Cursor routes the request to a model the team allows.

      if a model is blocked for the team, Cursor Router routes to an allowed model

    • A helper agent is set to a blocked model: The helper's configured model is not used when an admin has blocked it.

      a subagent's configured model is not used when an admin has blocked it

    Source entry: F07.model-allowlist. Each branch quotes the vendor's documentation word for word; the order between decision points is not stated.

  3. Load the house rules ◐ documented, with limits !

    Cloud agents read the project's instruction file, and the CLI and editor load project rules on their own. Rules can be scoped to file patterns and can include other files. User rules and project rules both go into the prompt, and team rules take precedence.

    Documented order: Team rules work alongside other rule types and take precedence over them.

    Decision point: Which rule wins when several rules apply?

    • A team rule overlaps another rule type: Team rules work alongside other rule types and take precedence.

      Team Rules work alongside other rule types and take precedence

    • Policy files sit at several folder levels: The closest applicable policy file has the highest priority for files under its folder.

      The closest applicable APPROVAL_POLICY.md has the highest priority for files under its directory

    • A higher-level policy meets a closer one: Higher-level policies still apply, unless they conflict.

      ancestor policies still apply unless they conflict

    Source entry: F03.precedence-scoping. Each branch quotes the vendor's documentation word for word; the order between decision points is not stated.

  4. Load memory and earlier sessions ◐ documented, with limits !

    It can keep notes between runs of an automation and save a learned rule from a pull request comment. You can continue, fork, rename and list past chats, and send a chat to a cloud agent, but uncommitted local changes do not go with it.

  5. Stock the built-in tools ● documented !

    The agent can edit files, search the code, run terminal commands and search the web. Terminal commands need your approval by default, and fetching a web page asks first unless the site is on an allow list. Searching without asking is off by default.

  6. Load skills and custom commands ◔ partly documented !

    Skills are folders of instructions the agent can pick when a task fits, or you can run one by typing a slash and its name. Commands are saved prompts kept at team, project or user level. The documentation does not mention per-skill tool or model overrides.

  7. Connect outside tools ◐ documented, with limits !

    It connects outside tools through MCP in the editor, the command line and cloud agents. Each connection needs approval, and each tool call needs approval unless pre-approved. The documentation gives conflicting answers on whether cloud agents accept one older connection style.

    Documented order: A connection is approved first; after that each tool call still needs its own approval.

  8. Set the safety posture ◐ documented, with limits !

    Terminal commands need approval by default. Run modes range from an allow list to an automatic reviewer, and a run-everything mode skips prompts. Plan, ask, debug and design modes exist. The new-folder trust question is off by default; a device policy overrides matching settings.

    Documented order: When a policy comes from device management, its value overrides the matching Cursor setting on the user's device.

  9. Pick the model and thinking effort ◔ partly documented

    You choose the model from a picker in chat or a command in the command line, and can set a default in settings. Effort levels depend on the model, and Composer has none. You can add your own key for a supported provider. The documentation does not mention shared model selection.

    Documented order: For the cloud agent interface, an omitted model choice falls back from the user default to the team default to a system default.

  10. Prepare an isolated workspace ◐ documented, with limits

    The command line can run the agent in a new Git worktree instead of your current checkout, and agents started that way from the agents window get a separate checkout. Helper agents share the parent's checkout by default. Worktrees are disabled for multi-root workspaces.

B. Each turn, before sending

For every request the harness decides what the model will read, and runs any code you asked it to run first.

  1. Assemble the prompt ◐ documented, with limits !

    Cloud agents let you choose the context window size, and a larger window can cost more. Automations use each model's maximum window with no toggle. Sensitive paths can be kept out of what the model reads, and a hook can block a file before it is sent.

  2. Run your own code at set moments ◐ documented, with limits !

    Hooks run your scripts at moments such as before a tool or shell command, after a file edit, or when a session starts or ends. A script can block an action. Hooks are set per user or per project, and project hooks run when the workspace is trusted.

    Decision point: Will a project's hooks run when I open the project?

    • The workspace is trusted: Project hooks load and run automatically when team members open the project.

      Project hooks load and run automatically when team members open the project in a trusted workspace

    • The workspace is not trusted: The documentation says the workspace must be trusted to run project hooks.

      the workspace must be trusted to run them

    Source entry: F06.trust-enable. Each branch quotes the vendor's documentation word for word; the order between decision points is not stated.

C. The model call

The harness sends the request and waits. This is the only step where the model itself does any work.

  1. Send the request and handle trouble ◐ documented, with limits !

    At the usage limit you see a notice and can switch on pay-as-you-go or upgrade. Auto uses a router that sends simple requests to fast models and complex work to the most capable ones. The documentation advises backing off with growing delays when rate limited.

  2. Set the thinking budget ◐ documented, with limits

    Which thinking options exist depends on the model. The command line can show the model's thinking blocks, and the cloud agent run stream sends thinking text. The documentation says thinking events are suppressed in print mode.

  3. Reuse the unchanged part of the prompt · not researched not yet researched

D. After the model answers, every turn

The model's answer is only a request. The harness checks it, runs it if allowed, and feeds the result back.

  1. Read what the model asked for · not researched not yet researched
  2. Decide whether it is allowed ◐ documented, with limits

    Rules decide what runs without a prompt, by tool, file pattern or command, and an automatic reviewer can check calls outside the sandbox. Allow lists are a convenience, not a security guarantee, and terminal commands can still read ignored files.

    Documented order: A terminal allow list, when set, overrides the in-app terminal allow list.

  3. Save an undo point ◐ documented, with limits

    Restoring a checkpoint on an earlier message rolls back the files the agent changed after that point, but the conversation keeps its messages. The command line can jump back to a previous message, and forking a chat from an earlier message shortens the conversation.

  4. Run it inside the fence ◐ documented, with limits !

    Commands can run in a sandbox that limits file and network access. Local agents run with the sandbox off by default and can reach the network without restriction. A command that fails inside it can be rerun outside, and a reviewer checks the rerun.

    Documented order: If a sandboxed command fails on a restriction, the agent can rerun it outside the sandbox, and a reviewer then checks that rerun.

    Decision point: What happens if the sandbox blocks a command the agent wants to run?

    • It fails on a sandbox restriction: The agent can rerun it outside the sandbox, and an automatic reviewer checks that rerun.

      the agent can rerun it outside the sandbox, and the classifier reviews that rerun

    • It needs full system access: It bypasses the sandbox; Cursor indicates this and asks for approval.

      Cursor indicates when a command runs outside the sandbox and asks for approval

    Source entry: F05.sandbox-override. Each branch quotes the vendor's documentation word for word; the order between decision points is not stated.

  5. Tidy the tool's output · not researched not yet researched
  6. Feed the result back and go round again ● documented !

    The agent calls a tool, reads the result and decides its next step. The documentation says there is no limit on the number of tool calls in a task. A stop hook can send a follow-up message to keep it going, with a default limit of 5.

  7. Hand work to helpers ◐ documented, with limits !

    Helper agents are set up as text files with their own model, tools and read-only choice, and several can run at once in their own context. The main agent and its direct helpers can start helpers; one started by another helper cannot start more.

  8. Shrink the context when it fills ● documented !

    When the window nears full, Cursor summarises older parts of the conversation to make room, and you can do it by hand with a command. A hook runs before compaction but cannot block or change it.

  9. Show the answer or ask you ◐ documented, with limits !

    Plan mode researches the code, asks clarifying questions and writes a plan you can edit before building starts. File editing is listed as allowed after you approve the plan. A status line and a context ring show progress and how full the window is.

  10. Wrap up and keep score ◐ documented, with limits !

    A spending dashboard shows the cost of requests, and you can fetch billed token use for an agent. You are asked to set a spend limit when you first use cloud agents. Usage metrics can stream to monitoring tools for Enterprise, and a command shows the debug log location.

    Decision point: What happens on a Teams or Enterprise plan when the Other Models allowance runs out?

    • On-demand usage is enabled: Own-key requests keep working.

      own-key requests keep working if on-demand usage is enabled

    • On-demand usage is off: Own-key requests stop until the next billing cycle.

      stop until the next billing cycle if it is off

    Source entry: F22.budget-caps. Each branch quotes the vendor's documentation word for word; the order between decision points is not stated.

E. Around the session

Things that sit outside a single turn: unattended runs, add-ons, updates and who runs the service.

  1. Run without you watching ● documented !

    Automations run cloud agents in the background on a schedule or when events arrive from tools such as GitHub, Slack and Linear. Cloud agents work in full development environments and keep going when your device disconnects. You can take over the remote desktop and hand it back.

    Decision point: How does the repeating prompt skill decide when to run?

    • An interval is specified: The prompt or skill runs on a recurring or variable interval.

      runs a prompt or skill on a recurring or variable interval

    • No fixed interval is given: The agent chooses when to wake.

      if you don't specify a fixed interval, the agent chooses when to wake

    Source entry: F15.scheduled-routines. Each branch quotes the vendor's documentation word for word; the order between decision points is not stated.

  2. Extend and share ◐ documented, with limits !

    Plugins bundle rules, skills, agents, commands, MCP servers and hooks. They install from the Cursor Marketplace, a Git repository or a local folder, and one repository can host several plugins. Marketplace plugins are manually reviewed before listing.

  3. Updates and releases ● documented !

    The command line tries to update itself by default, and there are Stable and Early Access channels. A device policy can switch updates off. Changelog pages list new features and fixes, and the documentation gives some deprecations as examples.

  4. Where it runs and who runs it ◐ documented, with limits

    Cursor is based on the VS Code codebase. The SDK, command line, editor and web app run the same agent, and SDK runs follow the same pricing and privacy rules as the editor. Tool calls can run on a customer's own workers while the agent loop stays in Cursor's cloud.

  5. Identity, retention and audit ◐ documented, with limits !

    Single sign-on is listed among team features, and a policy controls which team IDs can log in. Enterprise customers can enroll in US-only data residency, and a few models fall outside the data retention agreements. Admins are advised to review audit logs.
